362b561c4f5d2c55: The farmer-poet Wendell Berry once described a dystopian world where society is singularly directed toward “the objective” – a relentless drive for industrial extraction that leads to the destruction of nature and communities. The idea captured Berry’s concerns about the industrialization of agriculture and the expansion of natural resource extraction that became prominent across rural America in the latter decades of the 20th century. Over nine decades, Berry watched how agribusinesses’ and farm owners’ pursuit of productive efficiency and maximum profits led to machines and synthetic chemicals replacing human farm labor, and the replacement of diversified farms with monocropping and concentrated animal-feeding operations. Across the U.S., he saw small farms disappear, often consolidated into vast corporate businesses with absent owners. What gets lost in this pursuit of production and profit, he noted, are community, human dignity and flourishing, natural beauty and ecological well-being. People are the heart of rural towns, like Waubeka, Wis. Farm consolidation has shrunk many of America’s rural towns since the mid 1900s. AP Photo/Teresa Crawford As agriculture researchers and rural sociologists, we, like Berry, have seen how the industrialization of agriculture has changed the face of rural America and hollowed out its communities. Once-thriving main streets in rural towns have slowly lost their businesses, with fewer farm-related jobs to keep local residents in the area. Machine dealers and suppliers of farm input such as seeds, fertilizer and pesticides have disappeared. Local grocery stores have been replaced by gas station convenience stores. Schools have shrunk or consolidated with the population decline. Hospitals have closed. This “unsettling of America,” in Berry’s words, shows that the farm economy and the rural economy no longer rise and fall together. Rural communities continue to decline despite farm booms and busts. Losing farming’s rural economy multiplier effect Since the late 1940s, the number of farmers in the U.S. has plummeted by nearly 90%, falling from 5.9 million in 1948 to only 715,000 by 2025. During the same period, the agricultural workforce has shifted from mostly farm owners – about 78% – with a few hired hands in 1948 to one today where most of the work is done by farm laborers, about 68% of the workforce. This means profits from farming mainly flow to a small number of farm owners, while the people doing the farm work are paid much less. The loss of small, owner-operated farms, where a farm family could make a living, is one reason many rural communities have lost population over the past century. In prior eras, farming energized rural communities as money circulated in the rural economy, supporting rural businesses and populations – what is termed a “multiplier effect.” Today, local suppliers and services are harder to find, and farm profits instead flow to owners outside the community. Agriculture today resembles capital-intensive natural resource extraction, like mining, where a small number of very profitable businesses operate most acres in the county. Such farms employ few people at low wages, and profits accrue to distant landlords and investment firms. This shift further reinforces rural decline. The farm economy of the 21st century does little to create additional jobs in rural America. An analysis of 11 counties in Iowa found that every US$1 million of agricultural sales creates 2.4 total farm jobs and 1.6 spin-off jobs in other nonfarm businesses, for a total of four new jobs. By contrast, healthcare creates 10 new jobs and construction creates seven new jobs in all for every $1 million in sales. Both pay good wages, which keeps rural people from leaving and helps rural economies thrive. Both also create more spin-off jobs. In short, agriculture produces profits for the company, whereas healthcare and construction produce good-paying jobs for rural residents. More small farms can help communities thrive In the mid-1940s, the U.S. Senate commissioned two studies on the social impacts of economic concentration and corporate monopolies. In one, Walter Goldschmidt, an anthropologist at the University of California, Berkeley, described two agricultural communities in California, one with a few large farms and the other with numerous smaller farms. He evaluated the social qualities of each and found that the community with more small farms had a higher standard of living and quality of life than the community with a few large farms. The other study, overseen by Columbia sociology professor C. Wright Mills, compared urban manufacturing areas in the Midwest. It found that locations with many small companies had a more robust economic life, with higher socioeconomic well-being, than areas dominated by a few large firms. Many rural sociologists have tested these findings since then. One, a Cornell study led by rural sociologist Thomas Lyson, found a way to counter the effects of farm consolidation. Using U.S. Census of Agriculture and other county-level data, it found that communities with large-scale industrial-style farms that also had politically active populations and a high percentage of people running small, independent businesses tended to have higher levels of social well-being than those without. The effect of economic concentration Looking at the agriculture sector in 2026, it’s clear that policymakers have not listened to the concerns raised by Berry or the rural sociologists. According to the latest Census of Agriculture, America had fewer than 2 million farms in 2022. Fewer than 6% of those farms accounted for over three-quarters of all agricultural production. Farms are getting larger and more specialized. Economist Jim MacDonald documented that half of all cropland in 2017 was on farms with 1,445 acres, more than double the 650 acres in 1987. Half of all dairy farms had more than 1,300 cows in 2017, up from 80 in 1987. Half of all pig farms in 1987 marketed 1,200 pigs or more – the midpoint is currently over 50,000 pigs per year. The number of American farms fell while the size of those farms grew as consolidation became common across the country in the second half of the 20th century. USDA The supply chain is also shrinking, leaving farmers with fewer choices. Today, fewer companies control more of the markets where farmers buy their fertilizers and pesticides or sell their products, which means that farmers have less control over what they can raise or sell. For instance, just two companies accounted for 71.6% of the U.S. corn seed market in 2018-2022, and those same two companies accounted for 65.9% of the soybean seed market, according to USDA researchers. Twenty years earlier, the top two companies in those markets accounted for 47.2% of the corn seed market and 41.8% of the soybean seed market. When four or fewer firms control 40% or more of a market, farmers tend to pay more for seeds, fertilizer and pest control and receive less for their commodities, while consumers continue to face higher prices. Consolidation of land and commodity markets at the farm level often goes unnoticed and sometimes undocumented. University of Iowa economist Silvia Secchi describes how changes in the U.S. Census of Agriculture in 2002 and in 2017 “obfuscates the degree of consolidation” in the farm sector by allowing farms to report up to three or four farm operators. These changes have led to the official count of over 3 million farm operators, even though there are fewer than 2 million farms. By looking at the volume of sales, Secchi found that fewer than half of these 2 million farms produce commodities worth more than $1,000 annually. She contends that this way of counting farmers does a double disservice to small farm operators. First, it lumps disadvantaged farmers into a group that includes retired farmers and farmland owners who might be using their land as a tax write-off. Second, when the overall farm incomes are averaged, the inclusion of these small farmers make the large, high-value farmers appear to need more federal support. How to improve conditions in farm country Restoring the vibrant rural farm economy of the past may be unrealistic, but some policies could at least improve conditions. Devising new – and enforcing existing – antitrust laws to break up oligopolies and monopolies in the materials farms need, such as seeds and fertilizer, as well as in processing and trade could give farmers more choices about what to raise and where to sell it, while protecting consumers from high prices. Irrigated fields stretch for miles in many rural farming regions across the middle of America, including on Colorado’s eastern plains. Jim Wark /Design Pics Editorial/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) Right-to-repair laws could help farmers gain more control over their expensive machinery. Farm subsidies could be directed to smaller farmers who produce food – many of whom were inspired by Berry to become farmers – rather than toward the largest farmers who produce a few commodities at a massive scale. And finally, policymakers can develop rural policies that actually invest in the rural environment and communities, rather than simply subsidizing commodities in ways that primarily benefit the corporate owners of vast areas of farmland. 41496c8a0956b93d: Tech stocks are on a bumpy ride, weighed down by the slump in Nvidia's shares. Liu Yanan/Xinhua via Getty ImagesAfter stock markets, including the tech-heavy NASDAQ, got pummeled on Nov. 20, 2026, many Americans are asking themselves whether the huge bet on artificial intelligence is heading south. While markets rebounded the following Monday, this question still has profound implications for retirement savings, given how much these investment accounts are tied to stocks. Before Monday’s surge, the NASDAQ had plunged about 18% since early October and had lost more than US$4 trillion since Nov. 16. The broad-based S&P 500 also took a beating and had shed all its gains for the year. As a finance professor and certified financial planner, I can’t tell you whether the bubble has truly burst for good. But I can explain how the default model that most 401(k) plans use works, where it protects you, and what you might consider changing. Whether AI stocks recover or not, the steps that protect a retirement account are the same: Know what you own, keep the mix of assets in balance, and hold enough in savings and low-risk funds to cover the years when you’ll need it. Here are some basic facts to guide your planning. Many Americans are saving on autopilot Most 401(k) savers hold a target-date fund, which is named for the year of your “target” retirement and is often chosen as a default option by the employer. To understand how the current stock market volatility affects retirement savings, it’s important to first explain how these funds work. About 55% of U.S. families have a defined contribution retirement account, such as a 401(k) or an individual retirement account. And inside a 401(k), the investing is increasingly done for you. Six in 10 plans administered by the fund giant Vanguard signed workers up automatically in 2025 when they started a new job. And when those plans set a default investment, 98% of savers choose a target-date fund. About 60% of the nearly 5 million savers in those plans held a single target-date fund and nothing else. Taken together, target-date funds now hold $4.8 trillion. Inside each target-date fund is a list of index funds, which are named so because they track a particular market index. Vanguard’s series, the largest, is built mainly from four indices: U.S. stocks, international stocks, U.S. bonds and international bonds. The mix changes the older the saver gets, gradually moving away from high-return, high-risk stocks to safer, lower-yielding bonds. For example, Vanguard’s 2055 fund was just over 91% stocks at the end of September 2026, reflecting the relative youth of those holding it. That share drops to 16% for savers invested in the 2027 fund, who expect to retire imminently. The idea of target-date funds is that you can put your retirement savings on autopilot, with the mix of stocks and bonds getting more conservative the older you get. Brano on Unsplash Tech volatility is forcing new questions That autopilot model is now being tested, starting with Nvidia. In the span of a week, Nvidia went from riding the AI boom to getting mired in crisis. On Nov. 5, after the U.S. midterm elections raised the prospect of new curbs on AI and data centers, Nvidia shares fell more than 9%, while the broad-based S&P 500 index lost 4.4%. Then, on Nov. 12, Nvidia announced that CEO Jensen Huang had resigned. By the end of that week, Nvidia had lost more than $1 trillion in market value within a month. That slide may now be reversed. Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang on Nov. 23, causing its share price to soar. More broadly, it’s too early to say whether the AI bubble is over. Some analysts argue that it’s just losing some air rather than bursting. But amid the turmoil in tech stocks, savers may wonder whether a retirement plan on autopilot should adjust to this fresh volatility. Target-date funds have significant tech exposure Target-date funds are marketed as broadly diversified, often holding thousands of stocks, and financial advisers repeated that point after Huang’s exit. But those stocks aren’t held in equal amounts. Index funds weight companies by market value. So as the value of AI-linked companies soared, their share has grown in the funds most 401(k) savers hold. And that gets to the question of whether there’s a tech bubble riding on overvalued AI companies. By the end of 2025, the 10 largest companies made up nearly 41% of the S&P 500, according to RBC Wealth Management. Yet those 10, almost all of which are in tech and AI, were expected to produce only about 32% of the index’s 2025 earnings. In other words, investors are paying a premium for these shares because they’re expecting great profits later. Bad news can shrink that premium quickly. Savers should also know that a target-date fund dilutes the concentration of AI stocks, but it doesn’t remove them. At the end of September, the 10 largest companies made up 36% of Vanguard’s total U.S. stock fund, with Nvidia at 7%. A 2055 fund keeps about 55% of its money there. So roughly 20 cents of every dollar was riding on 10 companies, and about 4 cents on Nvidia. That means even a small drop in these stocks can have a big impact on your fund, depending on its asset mix. And while diversification hedges against one company’s turmoil, it’s less helpful if there’s a broad repricing of tech stocks. Even in Vanguard’s international fund, the four largest holdings are all tied to chipmaking, led by Taiwan Semiconductor, which makes Nvidia’s chips. Furthermore, diversification doesn’t mean guaranteed protection all the time. In 2008, during the global financial crisis, funds built for people retiring in 2010 lost nearly 24% on average. What to check now if you own a target-date fund In principle, savers don’t need to do anything as long as they choose to stay on autopilot until retirement. Fund managers buy and sell assets to stick to the target mix – a practice known as rebalancing. But rebalancing resets only the broad categories rather than trimming one particular company for growing too large. As Nvidia’s share of the market rose, so did its share of the fund. For people who hold just one target-date fund, I believe the right response to this month’s news is to leave their 401(k) account alone. The fund has been rebalancing all along, and your stake in any one company is modest. When markets are jumpy, savers should review the funds they hold and consider rebalancing toward lower risk if they’re close to retiring. Towfiqu Barbhuiya on Unsplash, CC BY But a saver still needs to check three things. First, consider the year you expect to retire. If you want to move it earlier or later, or want more or less risk, you should choose a fund with a different year. Second, look at what the fund’s share of stocks is today, which is on the fund’s fact sheet. If you’re 60 and your fund is 60% stocks, a 30% fall in stocks would cut your balance by roughly 18%. If that would derail your retirement plans, you can switch to an earlier-dated fund that holds less in stocks and brings less risk. Third, if you have other funds, you should review them. About 1 in 4 target-date investors in Vanguard plans hold other funds. If you add a tech fund or an S&P 500 fund, your account is riskier and more concentrated than the label suggests. What to do if you hold other funds About 31% of savers in Vanguard plans opt out of target-date funds and choose their own investments, perhaps because they find target-date funds too conservative or their fees too costly. For these investors, and for anyone with old 401(k)s and IRAs, there is more to do. Start by looking at the fact sheet for each fund, like this one for Vanguard’s S&P 500 index fund, and compare the top holdings. An S&P 500 index fund, a large-cap growth fund and a technology or Nasdaq-tracking fund look like three investments. But in fact you may own the same handful of companies three times. Next, you should rebalance your holdings according to your plan, not to a prediction. That means returning to the mix of stocks and bonds that you chose in the first place. Trades inside a 401(k) don’t trigger taxes, and many plans offer automatic rebalancing. If yours doesn’t, a simple rule backed by Vanguard research works: review once or twice a year, and rebalance whenever any part of your mix drifts more than about 5 percentage points from your target. Finally, consider broadening the stocks you own. Morningstar Indexes strategist Dan Lefkovitz has pointed to U.S. value stocks, smaller companies and international stocks as areas with less AI exposure. Your plan may offer funds for each. None of these makes you immune to losses, and diversifying can mean trailing the hottest part of the market for years. But the pattern can flip quickly: International stocks gained about 29% in 2025, far ahead of the S&P 500’s 16%. Align your savings to your timeline How much this month’s news matters depends on when you’ll need the money. If you’re decades from retirement, a downturn can work in your favor, because every paycheck contribution buys shares at lower prices. Keep contributing and capture your full employer match. My own research with a colleague has found that accounts on systematic investment plans akin to 401(k)s earned better market-adjusted returns than accounts funded with lump sums. If you’re within 5-10 years of retirement, the bigger danger is what planners call sequence-of-returns risk: A large loss right before or just after you start withdrawing can permanently shrink what your savings can support. A good defense is to hold several years of expected withdrawals in lower-risk assets, such as bonds or money market funds, so you’re never forced to sell stocks after a drop. For retirees, Morningstar’s Christine Benz suggests one to two years of withdrawals in cash and five to eight more in bonds. What not to do The costliest mistake is usually the most tempting: selling everything and waiting for the dust to settle. During the 2008-09 financial crisis, about 117,000 Fidelity 401(k) participants moved entirely out of stocks. Those who stayed out saw their balances grow just 2% by mid-2011, while those who kept some stock exposure saw balances rise 50% on average. Other moves to avoid include stopping your own 401(k) contributions, chasing whatever theme looks safe this month, and pulling money out early, which can mean taxes, penalties and a locked-in loss. Last, don’t hand the decision to a chatbot. It will likely give you sound general guidance, such as diversifying and not panic-selling, and that consensus advice is where AI is reliable. But it is weakest on high-stakes questions that turn on your own situation. 081efee3cb0ad95e: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 23 — As early as 7am, the grounds of Sekolah Menengah Kebangsaan (SMK) Batu Muda were already bustling with activity as parents prepared food packs and bottles of mineral water for candidates sitting for the 2026 Sijil Pelajaran Malaysia (SPM) written examinations.

Rather than simply dropping off their children for the first day of the examinations, parents arrived with a special mission — to ensure that every candidate was well-fed before entering the examination hall.
This is made possible through the “Food SPM” programme, an initiative organised by the school’s Parent-Teacher Association (PTA) for nearly seven years.

SMK Batu Muda PTA deputy chairman Mohd Aizam Talib, 52, said providing food on the school premises meant candidates did not have to leave the school compound to look for meals, allowing them more time to rest and revise before their next examination paper.

“This morning, about seven of us from the PTA provided mineral water, bread and traditional cakes (kuih) to keep the students energised. Later this afternoon, we will serve them a proper meal to ensure the examination schedule runs smoothly.
“We want the students to have enough time for a final revision before sitting for their afternoon paper,” he told Bernama at the school today.

He said the welfare initiative, which runs throughout the examination period, was made possible through the strong support of parents, who contributed both financially and through their voluntary efforts.

A committee member of the school’s PTA committee, Hasliza Ahmad Arif, 50, who helped coordinate the programme, said the presence of parents at the school was not merely to ensure candidates had enough to eat but also to boost the morale of students facing examination pressure.

The initiative holds special significance for her as her daughter, Nur Irdieena Soffia Sufian, is among this year’s SPM candidates. This makes caring for all 275 candidates a particularly meaningful responsibility for her, both as a mother and a PTA committee member.

“I am here to support my own child as well as all the students of SMK Batu Muda and help boost their spirits. Seeing parents around gives them a different level of motivation as they prepare to tackle their examination papers,” she said.

Apart from the PTA, the school’s parent support group, Kumpulan Sarana Ibu Bapa or KSIB, also joined the initiative, helping distribute snacks to candidates, particularly during short breaks between examination papers, to keep them energised.
KSIB member Norizan Idris, 47, said several parents, including herself, had taken time off work to help distribute food on a rotational basis throughout the examination period.
She said the initiative had become an annual tradition during examination season, serving as a gesture of care and moral support for all candidates.
“We care for these students as if they were our own children. We do not want anyone sitting for their examinations on an empty stomach. We want them to complete their papers with peace of mind.
“Once they have had something to eat and drink, we can see the relief on their faces,” said Norizan, who was also at the school to support her youngest child, another SPM candidate this year.

Earlier, Education Ministry Deputy Secretary-General (Management) Datuk Indera Ikmalrudin Ishak said the 2026 SPM examinations, which began today and will run until Dec 17, involve 21,425 candidates at 162 examination centres across the Federal Territory of Kuala Lumpur.
He also wished all candidates well, hoping they would sit their examinations calmly and achieve excellent results. — Bernama
12be677115429d8a: MADRID, Nov 23 — Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez seeks to thwart grim polls as polarised Spain holds an election on Sunday that could propel the opposition conservative Popular Party (PP) and the far right to power.
The outcome will be closely watched across Europe as it opens a cycle of elections over the next 12 months that could reshape the balance of power within the European Union.
Sanchez, who has become one of Europe’s best-known left-wing leaders after eight years in power, urged supporters this weekend to “vote, win and govern for four more years”.
But opinion polls still place him behind 65-year-old PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo, albeit by a narrowing margin.
“Spain needs change and together we are going to achieve it,” Feijoo told supporters, while urging them not to trust opinion polls.
The PP is predicted to win the most seats but fall short of a parliamentary majority, in a repetition of the hung parliament following the last general election in 2023.

Polls suggest its route to power lies with far-right, anti-immigration party Vox, parliament’s third-largest force, which could almost double its seats and make its leader Santiago Abascal a kingmaker.
Vox has campaigned heavily on immigration, with Abascal accusing migrants of living off benefits “that Spaniards need”.

Vox has formed coalitions with the PP in regional governments, but its presence in a national administration would be unprecedented for the far right since General Francisco Franco’s dictatorship ended in 1975.
Further complicating the situation for Sanchez is the weakness of other leftist parties whose support proved crucial to keep him in power in 2023.
Sanchez “must go now, out of decency and respect for the Spanish people. I don’t know if Feijoo is the right candidate, but we need a change”, businessman Pedro Suarez, 64, told AFP in Madrid.
Sanchez believes he can defy the predictions again. He has made escaping seemingly hopeless positions a hallmark of his career.
Spain ‘has moved forward’

His campaign has highlighted the dynamism of the European Union’s fourth-largest economy as well as social gains, notably for feminism and LGBTQ rights, that Sanchez says a PP-Vox coalition would reverse.

“This country has moved forward a lot in the past few years. A huge amount of things have been achieved on a social level,” said Pilar Sanchez, a 64-year-old former Madrid metro employee who intends to vote for the incumbent prime minister.
Sanchez has been described as Donald Trump’s nemesis, with Spain the only NATO member to defy the US president’s push to hike the alliance’s defence spending target to 5 per cent of GDP.
He is also the most senior Western leader to have sharply criticised Israel’s wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, earning him admiration in the Middle East and elsewhere in the Global South.

President of the Socialist International, Sanchez is one of few leftist leaders in the West and an outspoken champion of immigration as Europe lurched to the right with tougher measures on the hot-button topic.

Sanchez has tried to capitalise on anger over Spain’s chronic housing crisis, which catalysed the calling of a vote that was originally due in 2027, after the right voted down his minority government’s measures for tenants.
The opposition blames his successive governments for failing to stem spiralling housing costs.
‘Regeneration’
Feijoo, who ran the northwestern region of Galicia for 13 years, wants to project an image of experience and competence in his second attempt to win power.
He has spent years lambasting Sanchez over several high-profile corruption scandals, concessions to Catalan separatists and failing to pass a budget.
Other key PP attack lines are the migrant rush into the Spanish north African city of Ceuta in July and two high-speed train collisions this year that together killed 115 people.
Pensioner Victor Diaz, 85, told AFP that he viewed Sanchez as a “thief” but Feijoo as “a worker, like any other, working his whole bloody life without stealing”.

Pablo Simon, a professor of political science at Madrid’s Carlos III University estimated the number of undecided electors at around five million, adding that many were deciding late which way to vote.

But he described as a “myth” that they would swing the vote or that a high turnout automatically benefits the left, predicting more “fragmentation” with “stronger regionalist and nationalist parties”. — AFP
1baac713c73f31a7: KOTA BHARU, Nov 23 — A mother’s determination to motivate her autistic son has brought her back to the examination hall after more than two decades, as she sits for the Sijil Pelajaran Malaysia (SPM) examination alongside him today.

Mazlina Abdul Majid, 44, said she decided to retake the examination to ensure her eldest son, Muhammad Adam Danial Othman, 17, would not feel alone and to encourage him to strive for academic success.
She said her son had initially lost motivation to study, prompting her to register as an SPM candidate to foster a sense of healthy competition between them.
“I’m excited to sit for the SPM again, especially alongside my son. Initially, I just wanted to encourage him and give him the motivation and competitive spirit to study.
“Alhamdulillah, since I joined him, we’ve been able to revise together, and I can see that he’s become more motivated,” she told reporters at Sekolah Menengah Kebangsaan (SMK) Kota Bharu today.
Mazlina, who lives in Kampung Karang, Padang Bongor, Binjai, said balancing work and revision had been challenging, leaving her with only evenings to study.
She has worked as a dental surgery assistant at the Kota Bharu Dental Clinic for the past 20 years.
She said preparing for the examination was particularly demanding as she had made the decision at short notice, leaving insufficient time to cover the entire syllabus.
“I decided to retake the SPM around March and received approval from the department in May, so I only began preparing in June,” she said.
Mazlina relied heavily on YouTube learning materials and guidance from several teachers, including those at SMK Kota Bharu, while also attending private tuition, particularly for Mathematics.
Meanwhile, Muhammad Adam Danial said having his mother in the same examination hall gave him greater confidence.
The teenager, who is sitting for eight subjects, said his mother’s support, including their revision sessions at home, had helped him prepare for the examination.
“I’m nervous, but I’m doing this for my mother. I hope we can both succeed and achieve excellent results together,” he said.
Muhammad Adam Danial, who was diagnosed with autism while in Form Three, aspires to become a teacher and hopes his SPM results will bring him a step closer to fulfilling that ambition. — Bernama
1bc153e882cad765: BERLIN, Nov 23 — Borussia Dortmund coach Niko Kovac backed struggling winger Ethan Nwaneri to find form ahead of tomorrow’s Champions League clash at parent club Arsenal.
Nwaneri, 19, joined Dortmund on a season-long loan from the Gunners on deadline day, but has not been a beneficiary of the German club’s impressive start to the campaign.
Unbeaten in Germany this season, Dortmund sit two points clear of defending champions Bayern Munich atop the Bundesliga table.

But Nwaneri has just one assist in 13 appearances and has gone from being a regular starter to occupying largely a bench role, with some media outlets reporting the loan spell could end early in January.
Nwaneri burst onto the scene with Arsenal, becoming the youngest player in Premier League history when he made his debut aged 15 years and 181 days in September 2022.
The teenager scored 10 goals and laid on two assists in 51 matches for the Gunners, but moved to French side Marseille last season chasing more game time.
After scoring in his opening match, a 3-1 win over Lens in January, Nwaneri only netted once more during his time at the Ligue 1 club and was mostly relegated to the bench.
Clearly a fan of a fast start, Nwaneri assisted a goal in his opening Dortmund match but has yet to register another goal or assist.
He started his first five Bundesliga games for Dortmund but since then has not been named in the starting XI in any competition since mid-October.
During the recent international break, Nwaneri laid on two goals as England U21s beat France U21s 3-2.
‘Fierce competition’
Speaking on Thursday, Kovac praised Nwaneri’s performance for England and backed the teenager for a bright future, at Dortmund and beyond.
“Naturally, we look at the highlights,” Kovac said.
“We’re very pleased with him. He performed really well in a friendly match — he showed exactly why we signed him.”

The former Bayern and Monaco coach said Nwaneri would benefit from competing with Dortmund’s forward line, including Greek starlet Konstantinos Karetsas, Germany winger Maximilian Beier, veteran striker Serhou Guirassy and resurgent Portugal forward Fabio Silva.
“We have some very strong players in those attacking positions... There’s some fierce competition.”
Nwaneri moved to Dortmund seeking more game time to help him develop and deliver on his youthful promise and there are few clubs with a better record of incubating young talent.
Dortmund alumni Ousmane Dembele, Erling Haaland, Jude Bellingham, Achraf Hakimi and Robert Lewandowski have all either won the Ballon d’Or or finished near the top of the list in recent seasons.
Jude’s brother Jobe Bellingham, a teammate of Nwaneri in the England U21s, may be the next one off the Dortmund production line.
Jobe won a call-up to England’s senior squad in November for the first time, although he did not make it off the bench.

Despite not starting for Dortmund in recent weeks, a serious injury to Dortmund’s Italy forward Samuele Inacio could mean Nwaneri is in with a chance of more minutes against the Premier League leaders tomorrow.
Kovac said Nwaneri needed to be patient but that his time would come.
“He’s already played a good number of matches, and at just 19 years’ old, he’ll surely play many more for us during his time here,” the coach said.
Dortmund and Arsenal have not faced off in a competitive match since 2014, the season after the German side’s narrow loss to rivals Bayern in the Champions League final at Wembley.
In 2014/15, Dortmund and Arsenal both recorded 2-0 home victories in the old group stage.
The club’s most recent encounter was a 3-2 win for Dortmund over Arsenal in the pre-season Emirates Cup, with Nwaneri scoring the Gunners’ first. — AFP
dbba5b44c8e96c04: BANGKOK, Nov 23 — The collapse of marathon climate talks in Turkey has renewed questions about reform of their consensus requirement, and galvanised calls for legal action and ambitious side agreements between like-minded countries.

The “conference of the parties” talks, better known as COP31, ended without agreement and two days over schedule yesterday, as countries deadlocked on fossil fuels, finance, science and carbon-removing technologies.
It was an ignominious end for an unusual dual-presidency shared by Australia and Turkey, and negotiations chair Chris Bowen, who is Australia’s climate minister, said it was “very disappointing”.
For many observers, the outcome was the inevitable result of a process that has regularly been hamstrung by its insistence on consensus.

“Decision-making that requires every country to agree on every comma is not fit for a climate emergency,” said Nikki Reisch, director of the Centre of International Environmental Law’s climate and energy programme.
Bowen identified the same issue.
“The fundamental root of the problem is that when COP was created, for reasons I understand, it was made consensus only,” he said. “That’s a very tough ask.”
‘Significant reform’
Yesterday’s collapse has renewed calls for a reform to that consensus-based process, in which any one country, or a small minority, can nix progress.
“It has been clear for years that the COP process is in need of significant reform,” wrote former US vice president Al Gore on X.
He urged a “reinvigorated multilateral process that reflects the latest science and represents the will of the majority of the world.”
But as Bowen noted, “you also need consensus to change consensus” — in other words, all countries would have to agree those reforms.
He described that as a “particular challenge,” although others might characterise it as simply impossible.
The COP31 talks deadlocked over multiple issues, notably whether the so-called cover decision would mention phasing out planet-warming fossil fuels.
Several countries refused a deal without that mention, while others including Saudi Arabia were vehemently opposed to its inclusion.

There were other serious faultlines, including the timing of scientific work from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, and language on carbon capture, a technology championed by the fossil fuel industry but criticised by some as costly and ineffective.

Crucially for developing countries, there was also no progress on finance — the money badly needed to help countries transition energy systems and adapt to the natural disasters climate change is already worsening.

“The fundamental problem for globally agreed climate policy is more starkly obvious than ever: fossil fuel powers will not agree to have their resource wealth devalued, and rich countries won’t provide enough climate finance to the developing world,” said Frank Jotzo, professor of environmental and climate change economics at the Australian National University.
‘Doesn’t replace COP’
Other COPs have ended in failure before, including most recently in 2009.
But for all the forum’s failings, most agree that the COP process remains important for its unique format, bringing together virtually every country in the world and offering equal billing to all.
As a result, few suggest the process should be abandoned, but there are growing calls for alternatives to advance climate change action, including legal suits.
That route is already being pursued, most notably with an International Court of Justice advisory opinion that confirmed states have a binding legal obligation to combat climate change.

“If the negotiations are not delivering what individual states need, then they’ll certainly consider turning to the ICJ and other international courts,” said Harj Narulla, an international lawyer who advised the Solomon Islands at COP31.
Others expect growing interest in agreements made outside the COP process, like the Santa Marta initiative, bringing together countries committed to phasing out fossil fuels.
The process grew out of the COP30 meeting in Brazil, where interested nations sought to bypass a lack of consensus on the issue.
Members held talks earlier this year, and agreed some first steps, including an expert scientific panel to advise on pathways.
These “plurilateral processes are growing,” said Jotzo, and more are needed, including on carbon removal technologies and finance for adaptation.
Bowen too said he sees the Santa Marta process becoming “increasingly important.”
“Doesn’t replace COP. It’s just another way of doing it,” he added. — AFP

cc2adbe7a2fc82f3: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 23 — Oriental Kopi Holdings Bhd is expanding into Cambodia through a franchise agreement, marking its fourth overseas market as the Malaysian café operator seeks to build a regional business supported by recurring royalty income.

The ACE Market-listed group said today its indirect wholly-owned subsidiary, Oriental Coffee International Sdn Bhd, had signed a territory franchise agreement with Indochina Food and Beverage Co Ltd, granting the Cambodian company exclusive rights to develop and operate Oriental Kopi cafés nationwide.
Under the agreement, the first outlet is expected to open in Phnom Penh within 365 days, with expansion into other Cambodian cities to be explored subsequently.

The initial franchise term runs for five years from the opening of the first café and is renewable. Indochina will pay a franchise fee and monthly royalties, although financial terms were not disclosed.

The arrangement allows Oriental Kopi to expand without directly financing or operating the outlets, leaving its local partner responsible for site selection and day-to-day management. Oriental Kopi will supply its branding, recipes, operating systems and staff training while maintaining quality standards.
Cambodia, with a population of about 17 million, offers exposure to a young consumer market and a growing café culture.
The agreement follows Oriental Kopi’s entry into Indonesia and Mauritius in August, through a joint venture with Erajaya Group and a franchise arrangement with Coffee Time Ltd, respectively.
“Cambodia is our fourth overseas market, and the upcoming year will see these markets come on stream,” said managing director Calvin Chan Jian Chern.
He said the group expected its first Jakarta café to open at Central Park Mall by the end of 2026, followed by outlets in Mauritius and Cambodia.
Once operational, the expansion will give Oriental Kopi a presence in five countries, including Malaysia and Singapore.
Founded in 2020, Oriental Kopi currently operates 41 cafés, comprising 38 in Malaysia and three in Singapore. It also sells packaged products, including instant white coffee and kaya.

Oriental Kopi said the Cambodian agreement was unlikely to materially affect earnings per share, gearing or net assets for the financial year ending September 30, 2027, but was “expected to contribute positively to future earnings”.
98b7db1f57aadf85: A recent update broke attachment handling for some New Outlook users, prompting Microsoft to recommend switching to the web or Classic version of its email client.

Things are going swimmingly for New Outlook, the email client that Microsoft would very much like users to migrate to. A code change meant that for some users, opening or uploading email attachments failed. It took the company two attempts to fix the problem.

Microsoft confirmed there were issues on November 20, as reports that customers were having problems with attachments began rolling in. By the end of the day, the company had added inline images in email to the litany of woe and "paused the rollout of a recent client update that may be contributing to attachment failures."
The advice for affected users was to switch to the web version, or use Outlook Classic to open or upload attachments and view inline images.

The good news was that Microsoft produced a fix. The bad news was that this fix only resolved problems with Office attachments and inline images, leaving other attachment types affected, according to incident notice EX1561765.
The Windows behemoth tried again with a "supplemental fix" and reported the remaining problems resolved on November 21.
Users needed to close and reopen New Outlook for the fix to take effect.

Microsoft said it had tested the fixes before deployment. Administrators might reasonably wish the original update had received the same attention. The preliminary root cause was a "recent update to the code which supports embedded web content unexpectedly caused impact."

The clock is ticking for Outlook Classic. Microsoft is clear that New Outlook is the future, though Classic Outlook will remain available until at least 2029. The fact that the company had to suggest that affected users fall back on the old warhorse to perform that rarely used email activity – attachment handling – is less than confidence-inspiring.
Still, by the time Outlook Classic is finally put out to pasture, we're sure Microsoft's habit of sending out broken updates will also be a thing of the past. Right? ®
13d0c23472a04e8e: Microsoft has issued a critical vulnerability advisory after attackers were caught raiding Azure API Management (APIM) instances for secrets and performing admin operations.

According to a nonpublic advisory, seen by The Register, Microsoft said the attacks, which have already affected two major energy companies, only impact customers on Azure API Management Classic tiers, not Azure API Management v2.

It said of the now-patched vuln: "Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue."
Microsoft linked exposure to Classic-tier configurations that did not follow its network security guidance or stored secrets directly in APIM rather than referencing them from Azure Key Vault.
Microsoft directs customers to its security guidance for the recommended configuration.

The advisory lists potentially exposed secrets, including named values, client secrets associated with identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys, and tokens used to call direct management APIs.
Security expert Anders Kristiansen warned that stolen credentials could also give attackers access to services behind APIM.

"If someone obtains a credential from that configuration, they may be able to use it directly against the service it protects, outside APIM," he wrote. "What they can reach depends on the credential's permissions and whether it is still valid."
Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) urged organizations using APIM to assume their secrets and named values had been exposed and rotate all tokens and secrets.
The agency also advised mapping the information accessible through each APIM instance to assess the potential scope of any compromise.
NSM credited Norway's energy sector with first detecting the vulnerability last week. It named gas giant Equinor and hydropower company Skagerak Energi among the affected organizations.
The authority commended Equinor for its early detection and rapid information-sharing, and warned that growing use of AI increased the risk of further exploitation.

"The vulnerability affects several sectors in Norway and also beyond Norway's borders," it said. "NSM has close dialogue and cooperation with national and international partners and businesses about the situation.

"When a vulnerability becomes known, multiple actors will be able to attempt to exploit it. Rapid escalation in the use of artificial intelligence is affecting the situation. This poses a risk to Norwegian businesses."
Customers who spoke to The Register warned that forgotten development and test instances could leave more organizations exposed. The extent of exploitation remains unclear.
Microsoft said it identified the security issue on November 18 and automatically applied a mitigation to close the access path the following day.
The Windows giant said customers still needed to investigate whether their instances had been compromised before the mitigation was applied.
NSM nevertheless advised organizations to check their instance's runtime version against its published patch thresholds and contact their provider if it remained unpatched.
Microsoft did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®

She said the findings of the CMCF study will serve as the basis for determining whether additional protective measures or regulatory approaches suited to the Malaysian context are needed, taking into account industry developments, identified risks and the effectiveness of existing safeguards.
Teo said CMCF has held public consultations since September to develop a gaming subcode.

She said the consultations involve working groups comprising stakeholders such as operators, application and local and international game developers, online safety experts, the e-sports industry, legal practitioners and researchers.
“The feedback gathered through these public consultations will be considered to improve the subcode.
“Any need to review existing regulations will be assessed based on stakeholder feedback, current developments, identified risks and the effectiveness of the existing regulatory framework,” she said.
She said this approach ensures that regulations remain evidence-based and proportionate to risk, while prioritising user safety, particularly for children and teenagers.
Meanwhile, Teo said 202,402 items of fraudulent online content were taken down by service providers following requests from MCMC between Jan 1 and Nov 15.

On artificial intelligence company Anthropic’s claim that its technology was used in a political influence operation targeting users in Malaysia, Teo said the ministry is still awaiting further feedback from the company.

The Dewan Rakyat subsequently passed the 2027 operating and development expenditure estimates totalling RM2.613 billion allocated to the Communications Ministry under Budget 2027 by a voice vote, after 19 Members of Parliament debated the allocations.
dde208ed24f6c2a6: FRANKFURT, Nov 23 — Bomb threats were emailed to hundreds of schools across Germany today but there appeared to be no immediate danger, police said, after a wave of hoax warnings at schools across Europe in recent weeks.
Schools in the capital Berlin and the states of Baden-Wuerttemberg, Thuringia, Saxony-Anhalt and Rhineland-Palatinate were among those to report receiving the threats, authorities said.
In the southwestern state of Baden-Wuerttemberg alone, police said, more than 450 schools were sent the threats.
Police in all affected areas said they quickly concluded the threats did not represent a “concrete danger” and were “not serious”.
“There is no information indicating any specific danger or threat to the schools that received the emails or to any other schools,” Berlin police said.
However, some schools did evacuate as a precaution, local media reported.

Police in the western state of Rhineland-Palatinate said that in the “largely identical emails”, anonymous authors “claim to have placed explosive devices in school buildings and threatened to detonate them”.
Investigations were ongoing, they said, adding that such threats can cause “considerable uncertainty among the public” and constituted a criminal offence.
The tabloid Bild reported that the subject of the emailed threats was: “Death awaits you”.
An interior ministry spokesman said schools were not being advised to evacuate as the incident fits into “the current overall threat picture”.

“I think both the schools and the security authorities of the federal states are prepared for such incidents and can then respond in a way that is appropriate to the situation,” he told reporters in Berlin, declining to comment on who might be behind the incident.
In recent weeks, schools in Italy, Britain, Hungary and Serbia have been sent hoax bomb threats. It is not clear whether any of the incidents are connected.
There have also been hoax bomb alerts on flights across Europe and cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems in several European countries. — AFP
89062038c0dd4611: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 23 — Barisan Nasional administrations had previously given public funds to the Kuala Lumpur and Selangor Chinese Assembly Hall (KLSCAH), Minister in the Prime Minister’s Department (Federal Territories) Hannah Yeoh said today, as she pushed back against claims of preferential treatment over a nominal RM1,000 land premium granted to the heritage building.

ad025ce7499351fd: GENEVA, Nov 23 — Two 20-year-old chess grandmasters will contest the youngest-ever battle for the ultimate crown when the world championship gets under way tomorrow.
Indian defending champion Gukesh Dommaraju will face challenger Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan in a best-of-14 match in Geneva that could run until December 12.
“I don’t think I’m here to defend anything. I’m here to win it all over again. That’s the mindset I’m in,” Gukesh told reporters.
He said Sindarov was now “one of the very top players at the very top of his game, so for sure, it’s going to be a real test.
“I’m very enthusiastic for this match to test myself against such a strong player, and to see what I’m capable of.”
Sindarov is five months older than Gukesh, and both prodigies became grandmasters at 12.
Despite Sindarov being on a hot streak and the reigning champion having dipped in form, the challenger rated his chances of victory at 50-50.
Sindarov said he had been playing plenty of matches over the past six months, “but still, it’s maybe not enough to prepare for such a hard tournament”.
Each daily match can last several hours. With a win scoring one point and a draw a half point, the first player to reach 7.5 points wins the match.
If the contest is tied at 7-7, the title is decided on a tie-break.
The total prize fund is US$2.5 million (RM10.3 million). The players earn US$200,000 for each game they win, with the remainder split equally.
Swiss chocolate chess pieces
Aged just 18, Gukesh beat Chinese title holder Ding Liren in the 2024 world championship in Singapore, becoming the youngest undisputed world champion.
Sindarov earned his spot in Geneva by winning the eight-player Candidates Tournament in Cyprus in April.
Sindarov is peaking at fourth in the global rankings, while Gukesh has dropped to 26th. Norway’s Magnus Carlsen remains the number one.
The championship’s opening ceremony was held yesterday in the Assembly Hall at the United Nations in Geneva.
Two Swiss clocks were brought on the podium containing giant chocolate knights — one white and one dark.
Gukesh chose one clock, revealing the dark knight inside, meaning Sindarov will play white in the first game and have the opening move.
The match will be played at the Fondation Martin Bodmer overlooking Lake Geneva.
The museum and library, which traces the evolution of human thought and literature, contains manuscripts, first editions, rare books and archaeological treasures.
Both players studied the venue on Saturday.
“I checked the chairs, the lighting, the floor — different kinds of things that can bother you during a game,” said Gukesh.
AI fuelling chess growth
While Sindarov has been getting plenty of match practice in tournaments, Gukesh has been focusing on the title clash.
“When you play a world championship, it’s very nice that it’s just one opponent, so you can put full attention on one specific player,” he said.
“There’s a lot of analysing your opponent going on,” he said.
Sindarov praised Gukesh’s ability to “fight until the end”.
“He has a very good strength in some typical positions. His calculation is very good,” the Uzbek said.
International Chess Federation (FIDE) president Timur Turlov said “chess is on the rise”.
“We are standing closer and closer to the point where we can become a very commercially successful global sport,” he predicted.
He said the growth of digital chess and easily-accessible coaching using artificial intelligence would drive the game forward and create the next generation of stars. — AFP
90ee1286527901e5: Software e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has admitted that hackers stole customers' card numbers and CVV security codes, raising questions about how the attackers captured data that payment security rules prohibit retaining after authorization.

The Germany-headquartered company, which handles software sales and subscriptions on behalf of other businesses, detected unauthorized activity on its platform on November 4. In an incident update, Cleverbridge said it had cut off the intruders' access and launched an investigation that later established payment card information had been copied from its systems.
The public notice doesn't spell out exactly what was stolen, but an email sent to affected customers, seen by The Register, fills in some rather important blanks.

"Based on our investigation to date, the information involved includes payment card details you used to make a purchase through Cleverbridge, notably your card number, expiry date, card security code (CVV/CVC), and contact details," the company told customers.
Email addresses, billing addresses, and phone numbers were also among the information potentially exposed, although Cleverbridge reckons account passwords escaped the breach.
More concerning are the stolen CVV codes. PCI DSS rules prohibit retaining card verification codes after authorization, even in encrypted form.

Cleverbridge hasn't explained how the attackers obtained the codes, whether they were retained after transactions, or whether the criminals intercepted them during payment processing. The company didn't respond to The Register's questions about the breach.

Cleverbridge handles the business of selling software online, from taking payments to managing subscriptions, and its client roster includes some familiar names in enterprise IT, such as Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Parallels, and Plesk.

That doesn't mean customers of all those companies had their card details stolen. Cleverbridge hasn't named the vendors affected by the intrusion, nor has it disclosed how many people were caught up in the breach or how long the hackers were poking around its systems.

In its notification to customers, the company said it had contacted data protection authorities, payment card schemes, and its payment partners, and was working with a specialist police cybercrime unit. It began notifying affected individuals on November 20, more than two weeks after discovering the intrusion.

Affected customers are being offered 24 months of free credit monitoring and fraud assistance. That may help detect identity misuse, but it won't stop a crook armed with their card number, expiration date, and CVV from attempting a fraudulent purchase.
Two years of credit monitoring is a nice gesture, but customers whose card numbers and CVVs are now in criminal hands might prefer a new bit of plastic. ®
265a959c3f501c4d: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 23 — A reproduction of a Pablo Picasso artwork linked to the 1Malaysia Development Bhd (1MDB) case will be featured in a special exhibition space at the Malaysia Art Ecosystem Fair (MAEF) 2026, to be held at the Kuala Lumpur World Trade Centre from Nov 27 to 29.

826a7abd8a45293a: NOVEMBER 23 — A child who builds an imaginary city using cardboard boxes may be demonstrating remarkable creativity. Another who comforts a crying classmate may be showing emotional maturity beyond their years. A third who struggles to complete a written test may be exceptionally good at solving practical problems. Yet, how often do these abilities find their way into a school progress report?

We often speak about preparing children for the future, equipping them with creativity, critical thinking, communication skills and emotional intelligence. However, an important question remains. Are the ways we assess our children keeping pace with the very skills we claim to value? For decades, we have relied heavily on written exercises, examinations, grades and standardised measures to determine children’s progress. These methods certainly have their place. However, a child’s development is far too complex to be captured through numbers alone.

Consider a seven-year-old who cannot write a perfect paragraph but can confidently narrate an imaginative story. Or a child who takes longer to complete mathematical exercises but instinctively understands how to divide toys fairly among friends. Should we consider these children less capable simply because their abilities are not easily measured through conventional assessments? Perhaps the problem is not that children lack abilities. Perhaps we have become too accustomed to looking for those abilities in the wrong places.

Assessment in today’s classrooms should be as creative and diverse as the children themselves. Instead of constantly asking children to demonstrate what they remember, we should create opportunities for them to show what they can do, how they think and how they interact with others.

Imagine assessing mathematical understanding through a classroom mini-market where children become buyers and sellers. They count money, calculate prices, negotiate and make decisions. A teacher can observe not only their numeracy skills but also their communication, confidence and ability to solve problems. Similarly, language development need not always be assessed through worksheets and spelling tests. Storytelling, puppet shows, role-playing and simple conversations can reveal a child’s vocabulary, imagination, listening skills and ability to express ideas.

Even a playground can become a meaningful assessment environment. When children negotiate the rules of a game, settle disagreements or include a classmate who has been left out, they demonstrate social and emotional competencies that are rarely reflected in academic grades. These moments should not be overlooked merely because they cannot be conveniently converted into percentages.

Technology can also contribute meaningfully to this transformation. Digital portfolios containing photographs of children’s creations, short audio recordings of their reflections and samples of their work can help teachers and parents observe developmental progress over time. However, technology should document authentic learning rather than replace it. Artificial intelligence may assist teachers in organising observations, but it should never become the sole judge of a child’s abilities.

Importantly, creative assessment does not mean abandoning academic standards or allowing children to do whatever they please. It requires teachers to establish clear developmental goals, observe children systematically, document evidence and provide meaningful feedback. A well-designed play-based assessment can be just as rigorous as a written test, provided that teachers know precisely what they are assessing.

Malaysia’s continuing curriculum and assessment reforms present an opportunity to rethink how we define children’s progress. Classroom-based assessment should become more than another administrative responsibility. Teachers need sufficient professional development, manageable workloads and practical assessment tools to evaluate children’s cognitive, physical, social, emotional and creative development in meaningful ways.

Parents, too, must reconsider their expectations. A report card filled with excellent grades may be reassuring, but it does not necessarily tell us whether a child is curious, resilient, compassionate or capable of working with others. We should be equally interested in how our children respond to setbacks, express their feelings, ask questions and contribute to their communities.

After all, childhood is not a race to see who can read first, calculate fastest or achieve the highest marks. Children develop at different rates, possess different strengths and deserve opportunities to demonstrate their abilities without constantly being compared with one another. Perhaps our education system needs to ask a different question. Instead of merely asking whether a child has achieved the expected score, why not ask what the child can do today that they could not do yesterday? That, surely, is a more meaningful indication of development.

If we genuinely want children to grow into creative, confident and compassionate individuals, we must first have the courage to assess more than what can be written on an examination paper. A child’s potential is far greater than the space provided on a report card.*Assoc. Prof. Dr. Mohd Isha Awang and Assoc. Prof. Dr. Muhammad Noor Abdul Aziz are from the School of Education, Universiti Utara Malaysia (UUM).** This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.

8574c0c7162cc630: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 23 — The High Court was told today that the Government’s valuation for acquiring 263.272 acres from Semantan Estate (1952) Sdn Bhd, known as the Duta Enclave, in 1956 complied with the Land Acquisition Act and Malaysian Valuation Standards.

Tan Tat Khuan, 40, assistant director of the Ministry of Finance’s Valuation and Property Services Department, testified that his valuation recommended compensation for land value only, unlike Semantan Estate’s claim, which covers both land value and compensation for severance and injurious affection (adverse effects from the acquisition).
“The plaintiff’s valuer assessed the land at RM1.5 million; my valuation is RM875,000. Why do I say the plaintiff’s valuation is inaccurate?
“Among the reasons is that he relied on comparable or land transaction evidence after the Dec 3, 1956 acquisition, which is not permitted by the First Schedule of the Land Acquisition Act.

“Furthermore, all the comparables by the plaintiff’s valuer were bungalow lots in Kenny Hill (now known as Bukit Tunku), whereas in this case the subject matter is a large tract of land with development potential.
“Other factors such as access and land use were also not taken into account in his valuation, resulting in an excessively high value,” he said.
Tan, the Government’s sole witness, was responding to a question from Justice Roslan Mat Nor at the hearing on the compensation assessment for the Duta Enclave today.
In earlier proceedings, Tan informed the court that in 1965, the Government of Malaysia paid RM1.39 million in compensation to Semantan Estate, higher than the RM875,000 he had recommended.
Justice Roslan also asked Tan whether the valuation submitted by the plaintiff conflicted with any established land valuation practice.
The witness replied that the plaintiff’s selection of comparable evidence contravened the Land Acquisition Act as well as a Federal Court decision on the method for valuing large tracts of land.

“In my rebuttal report, I explained that the selection of comparables contravened the Land Acquisition Act and a Federal Court decision holding that the valuation of large agricultural land cannot rely on bungalow plots as comparables.
“In a Johor case cited in my rebuttal report, the Federal Court ruled that residential plots cannot be used in the valuation of agricultural land,” he said.
At today’s proceedings, senior federal counsel Azza Azmi appeared for the Government, while counsel Ira Biswas appeared for Semantan Estate. The hearing resumes in March next year.

On Nov 13, 2025, the Federal Court dismissed Semantan Estate’s application for leave to appeal against the Court of Appeal’s decision that the Registrar of Titles for the Federal Territory need not register the 263.272-acre parcel in the Duta Enclave in the company’s name.

The Court of Appeal’s decision in the Government’s favour therefore stands, as the company cannot pursue its appeal to the Federal Court, and the case was remitted to the High Court for a hearing on compensation assessment.

On June 24, 2025, the Court of Appeal ruled that Semantan Estate is not entitled to ownership of the land, but is entitled to reasonable compensation based on the land’s value in 1956, when the Government took it over.

The land, in prime Jalan Duta, houses the Inland Revenue Board headquarters, several government buildings, the National Hockey Stadium, the Institute of Islamic Understanding Malaysia and the Federal Territory Mosque, among others.
In 2003, Semantan Estate filed suit against the Government alleging trespass arising from the unlawful acquisition of the land from the company.

In 2009, Judicial Commissioner Zura Yahya ruled that Semantan Estate retained its beneficial interest in the 263.27-acre parcel, which had been unlawfully acquired by the Government, and that the Government had trespassed on the land. — Bernama

8e2d81bc0adc1e65: JAKARTA, Nov 23 — Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto put forward yesterday two candidates to succeed Gibran Rakabuming Raka, who has resigned as vice president following a scandal over his high school diploma.

Gibran’s resignation on November 12, after a Supreme Court ruling annulled his overseas high school qualification, has added to pressure on a government facing widespread dissatisfaction over the economy, graft and wildfires.
The former vice president is the son of Prabowo’s predecessor and political rival Joko Widodo, whose popularity is widely seen to have helped the incumbent to the top job.
Prabowo submitted yesterday the names of two candidates for parliament to consider, speaker of the People’s Consultative Assembly Ahmad Muzani told reporters.
Lawmakers will convene on December 11 to select between Agriculture Minister Andi Amran Sulaiman and former foreign minister Sugiono, who is the ruling party’s secretary-general.
“I believe that both of them will do their best for the nation, the state, and the people of Indonesia,” Prabowo told reporters.
Sugiono, who like many Indonesians uses only one name, is sometimes referred to as the president’s “ideological child” due to their close working relationship.

A vice president from Prabowo’s party could help “secure the popularity” of the president ahead of a potential re-election bid in 2029, Centre for Strategic and International Studies researcher Dominique Nicky Fachrizal told AFP before the nomination.

The 47-year-old Sugiono, who had a short stint in the army’s special forces unit before retiring in 2004, was made coordinating minister for human development and cultural affairs in a cabinet reshuffle last month.
Andi, 58, was a businessman before serving as the agriculture minister under Widodo, also known as Jokowi, between 2014 and 2019.
He returned to the post following a corruption scandal involving his successor, and was re-appointed when Prabowo came to power in 2024. — AFP
bdc2940ce0c223c4: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 23 — Malaysia and Pakistan are committed to strengthening defence and security cooperation, including through trilateral cooperation with Türkiye, while exploring opportunities for collaboration in maritime security and counterterrorism efforts.

Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said in a Facebook post today that the matters were discussed during a courtesy call by Pakistan’s Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir.

He said the meeting also provided an opportunity to exchange views on regional and international security developments, including efforts to ease tensions in West Asia and the importance of safeguarding global maritime security.
According to him, the discussions also touched on the need to prioritise dialogue and restraint in addressing border tensions while respecting national sovereignty and protecting civilians.

12e09cfb44a79fe8: Capita CEO Adolfo Hernandez has stepped down with immediate effect as the outsourcer warned of sharply lower profits next year, nearly a year after its troubled takeover of administration of the UK's Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS).
In a statement, Capita said CFO Pablo Andres had become CEO, with group financial controller Gemma Bate-Williams succeeding him as finance chief.

Capita now expects adjusted operating profit for 2027 to be £85 million to £95 million below previous expectations. That includes £15 million to £25 million in additional costs under a pensions recovery plan agreed with the Cabinet Office, alongside pressure from contract exits and other trading headwinds.
Shares fell around 70 percent following the announcement.

The company – which is also coming under fire for its £370 million contract with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) – said it had made significant progress in its transformation and strategic simplification. It also plans to raise around £190 million through a share issue in the first half of 2027 to reduce borrowing and to "allow the business to move forward from a more stable foundation," subject to support from its financial creditors.

James Preece, principal analyst at UK tech research firm Megabuyte, said: "Slow motion car crash comes to mind. It has been a turnaround job for coming up to four years now, with long-suffering shareholders watching dozens of disposals and business exits fail to arrest a structural decline in both margins and growth.

"Today's update suggests that management's underlying forecast assumptions alongside other more transient factors were still too punchy, and the leverage situation now calls for action. The share price reaction suggests confidence in this being a one-and-done raise is limited," he said.

Capita took over administration of the scheme in December 2025 under a seven-year, £239 million contract, after which The Register exclusively revealed problems with its online systems. The vendor promised AI and automation, but the takeover brought a glitchy online portal, while some members struggled to receive pension payments. By January, it was clear the service was seriously failing, leaving some retired civil servants struggling to make ends meet.
Capita missed its deadline to restore normal service by the end of June. It subsequently told MPs that all but the most complex cases would return to normal service by September.
The pensions scheme serves around 1.7 million members. Media reports and MPs have described members feeling upset, frustrated, and ignored, with some waiting months for payments.

The government said it had withheld £10 million in payments over Capita's performance during the transition of the pensions service and was negotiating further penalties. It also appointed an auditor to assess the case for further penalties for Capita's performance on the contract.

Last month, the National Audit Office launched an investigation into the CSPS contract. Responding to the investigation, Capita said it "accepts that performance remains below the standards that scheme members and the Government rightly expect" and that fixing the problems was its top priority.

The Public and Commercial Services Union is campaigning to get the government to scrap a separate Capita contract, the Synergy shared services deal, which Capita values at £370 million. The deal covers HR, payroll, finance, and other back-office services across four government departments and nearly 100 arm's-length bodies. Rival bidder Sopra Steria, which owns incumbent provider SSCL, has also launched a legal challenge alleging Capita's bid was abnormally low. Capita and the DWP – which leads on the contract – have denied the allegations. ®
